items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: What about fairness, bias and discrimination?
items.publisher: Information Commissioner's Office
items.locator: Sections 'Why might an AI system lead to discrimination?', 'Should we just remove all sensitive data?', 'Can we process special category data to assess and address discrimination in AI systems?'
items.why: Imbalanced training data and data reflecting past discrimination; why removing sensitive fields fails (occupation, working hours, postcode as proxies); worked example relying on Article 9(2)(g) with Schedule 1 paragraph 8. Carries a banner: under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.
items.quote: simply removing special category data (or protected characteristics) does not guarantee that other proxy variables cannot essentially reproduce previous patterns

items.title: AI tools in recruitment: audit outcomes report
items.publisher: Information Commissioner's Office
items.why: Source of the quotation (p.3) and the figure (p.12). Pages 18-20 cover training and testing data: not all providers sampled for representative datasets; some 'cleaned' data of demographics and proxies. Page 22: inferred characteristics are still special category data and need a condition.
items.quote: not all had used sampling techniques to ensure datasets were diverse and representative of the relevant population

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018, Schedule 1, paragraph 8: Equality of opportunity or treatment
items.publisher: legislation.gov.uk
items.locator: Sch.1 para 8(1)-(5); see also para 5 (appropriate policy document)
items.why: The UK condition for processing special category data to review equality of opportunity. Four categories only (racial or ethnic origin, religious or philosophical beliefs, health, sexual orientation); not for decisions about a particular person; not if likely to cause substantial damage or distress; stops on written objection.
items.quote: identifying or keeping under review the existence or absence of equality of opportunity or treatment between groups of people

items.title: Equality Act 2010, section 19: Indirect discrimination
items.publisher: legislation.gov.uk
items.why: The effect-based test: a practice that puts a protected group at a particular disadvantage is discriminatory unless a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim. No exception for the state of the data.
items.quote: it puts, or would put, persons with whom B shares the characteristic at a particular disadvantage

items.title: Responsible AI in Recruitment
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.why: Supports asking the supplier what data trained the model, with a breakdown by protected characteristic and source; states that historical bias in training data is perpetuated at scale; bias audits to be repeated at intervals.
items.quote: If there are historical biases in this data, then the tool is likely to perpetuate these biases at scale.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 9: Processing of special categories of personal data
items.publisher: legislation.gov.uk
items.quote: processing is necessary for reasons of substantial public interest
items.why: The prohibition a bias check has to get past. Data on race, religion, health or sexual orientation cannot be processed, even to look for bias, unless an Article 9(2) condition applies; point (g), substantial public interest on a basis in domestic law, is the one the equality-monitoring condition in the Data Protection Act 2018 hangs from. Sex and age are not special category data, so this hurdle does not apply to them.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018, Schedule 1, Part 4: Appropriate policy document and additional safeguards
items.publisher: legislation.gov.uk
items.quote: requires the controller to have an appropriate policy document in place when the processing is carried out
items.why: The paperwork behind 'bias-detection processing is used deliberately and lawfully'. An organisation relying on the equality-of-opportunity condition must have a policy document explaining how it complies with the data protection principles and how long the data is kept. The approved brief cites the requirement through paragraph 5; this is the Part that defines it.

items.title: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), Article 10: Data and data governance
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: Training, validation and testing data sets shall be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete
items.why: The only binding rule read that requires data to be examined for bias before use: providers of high-risk systems must examine data sets for biases likely to lead to prohibited discrimination and take measures to detect, prevent and mitigate them. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text as at 27 July 2026; paragraph 1 is marked amended and paragraph 5 deleted by the Digital Omnibus. EU law, on providers of high-risk systems; no direct effect in the UK. Application dates are not stated here.

items.title: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), Article 4a: Processing of special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: the bias detection and correction cannot be effectively fulfilled by processing other data, including synthetic or anonymised data
items.why: The EU's lawful route for using sensitive data to find bias, to set beside the UK's Schedule 1 paragraph 8. Narrower in one way (strictly necessary, and only where synthetic or anonymised data will not do; deletion once the bias is corrected) and wider in another (paragraph 2 extends it to deployers and to systems that are not high-risk). Added by the Digital Omnibus and marked NEW on the Commission's copy of the consolidated text as at 27 July 2026; the former Article 10(5) is shown there as deleted. EU law only.

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: Annex A, Fairness in the AI lifecycle
items.publisher: Information Commissioner's Office
items.locator: Sections 3 (Data collection) and 4 (Data analysis and pre-processing), 'What is statistical bias?'
items.quote: your training dataset is not representative of the population that you will eventually apply your trained model to
items.why: The regulator's stage-by-stage account of how bias enters data: unrepresentative samples, features measured less accurately for some groups, labels that carry past prejudice, and target variables that stand in for a protected characteristic. It tells buyers to ask dataset suppliers how the data was collected. Carries the banner: under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. Data protection only; it says it does not cover equality law.

items.title: Research Note: A literature review on bias in supervised machine learning
items.publisher: Financial Conduct Authority
items.locator: PDF p. 11 (proxies; training only on accepted applicants, p. 12); numbered findings, PDF p. 7
items.quote: seemingly unrelated characteristics might be close proxies for demographic characteristics or characteristics of vulnerability
items.why: The financial regulator's own review of the research on where bias comes from in financial services models: historical bias in data, proxies, and training only on applicants who were accepted before. A recent UK source outside recruitment. A staff research note, which states it may not represent the FCA's position; a literature review, not guidance, and it sets no expectation of firms.

items.title: Review into bias in algorithmic decision-making
items.publisher: Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation
items.locator: Chapter 2, summary box ('Fairness through unawareness is often not enough to prevent bias'); Recommendation 6
items.quote: ignoring protected characteristics is insufficient to prevent algorithmic bias and it can prevent organisations from identifying and addressing bias
items.why: Official UK support for the brief's point that deleting the sensitive column is no remedy: the review found that leaving protected characteristics out neither prevents bias nor lets an organisation find it, and recommended clear guidance on collecting such data for monitoring. Advisory; dated 2020, before the current law on automated decisions.

items.title: Enabling responsible access to demographic data to make AI systems fairer
items.publisher: Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation
items.quote: Using proxies does not avoid the need for compliance with data protection law.
items.why: On the practical obstacle to screening data: organisations often do not hold the demographic data needed to look for bias. The report weighs two ways round it, trusted intermediaries and inferring characteristics from proxies, and warns that inference can be inaccurate and is still personal, often special category, data. It is more open to careful use of proxies than the regulator's 2024 audit; the two should be read together. Advisory; predates the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.

items.title: Ensuring statistical models command public confidence: Learning lessons from the approach to developing models for awarding grades in the UK in 2020
items.publisher: Office for Statistics Regulation
items.locator: Findings, 'Understanding the impact of historical patterns of performance in the underlying data on results'
items.quote: The previous history of grades would have included patterns of attainment that are known to differ between groups.
items.why: The official review of the 2020 exam-grading models: a UK case of historical data carried into decisions about individuals. Each centre's past results were a major input, and there was little public discussion beforehand of the patterns in that data. The review also records that the regulators' equality analyses found attainment gaps did not widen; its finding is about confidence and transparency, not proven discrimination. Statistical models, not machine learning. This is the summary page; the full report (PDF) was not read.

items.title: Equity in Medical Devices: Independent Review
items.publisher: Department of Health and Social Care (independent review chaired by Professor Dame Margaret Whitehead)
items.locator: Executive summary, Recommendation 10 (PDF p. 19); chair's foreword (PDF pp. 6-7)
items.quote: should ensure they are transparent about the diversity, completeness and accuracy of data through all stages of research and development
items.why: A government-commissioned independent review that found unfair bias in medical devices, including from unrepresentative datasets in AI algorithms and testing in mainly White populations. Its recommendation on data applies to those deploying AI devices as well as those building them. Health sector only; recommendations to government, regulators and the NHS, not binding rules.

items.title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard: guidance for public sector bodies
items.publisher: Government Digital Service
items.locator: Section 11, Development Data Specification, 'What are sensitive attributes?'
items.quote: any information that may be closely correlated to unobserved personal attributes or protected characteristics
items.why: A government standard that makes proxy screening a matter of record: for each tool, bodies are asked to disclose the personal data attributes, protected characteristics and proxy variables in the development data. Mandatory for government departments and for arm's-length bodies that deliver public services, for tools in scope. A transparency record, not a test: it asks what is in the data, not whether it is biased. The date is that of the latest update shown on the page.

items.title: Towards a Standard for Identifying and Managing Bias in Artificial Intelligence (Special Publication 1270)
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (US)
items.locator: 'Statistical and Computational' bias (PDF p. 18); systemic bias (PDF p. 15); proxies (PDF p. 25)
items.quote: Statistical and computational biases stem from errors that result when the sample is not representative of the population.
items.why: Sets out three categories of bias (systemic, statistical and human) and says systemic or historical bias is present in the datasets AI uses. Gives United States examples of proxies, such as race inferred from zip code. A NIST special publication dated March 2022: guidance towards a standard, voluntary, United States context.

items.title: Model Artificial Intelligence Governance Framework, Second Edition
items.publisher: Info-communications Media Development Authority (IMDA) and Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC), Singapore
items.locator: Section 3, Operations management: 'Data for model development', 'Minimising inherent bias' (PDF pp. 38-39)
items.quote: Premature removal of data attributes can make it difficult to identify and address inherent bias.
items.why: International comparator. Singapore's voluntary framework asks organisations to know where data came from (data lineage) and to look for selection and measurement bias in it, and gives the same warning as the UK regulator: stripping attributes out too early makes bias harder to find. Voluntary; Singapore; second edition, 2020.

items.title: Using sensitive data to prevent discrimination by artificial intelligence: Does the GDPR need a new exception?
items.publisher: Marvin van Bekkum and Frederik Zuiderveen Borgesius (arXiv; Computer Law & Security Review 48 (2023) 105770)
items.quote: We argue that the GDPR does prohibit such use of special category data in many circumstances.
items.why: Peer-reviewed analysis of the tension at the heart of this criterion: checking a system for discrimination needs data on ethnicity and similar characteristics, which data protection law restricts. The authors conclude that the EU GDPR blocks such use in many cases and weigh the case for a new exception. Useful contrast: the UK already has one, in Schedule 1 paragraph 8 of the Data Protection Act 2018, and the EU has since added Article 4a of the AI Act. European law; written when the AI Act was still a proposal. Only the abstract was read.

items.title: Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial Gender Classification
items.publisher: Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru; Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 81 (Conference on Fairness, Accountability and Transparency)
items.quote: these datasets are overwhelmingly composed of lighter-skinned subjects (79.6% for IJB-A and 86.2% for Adience)
items.why: Peer-reviewed evidence of who is missing from data and what follows. Two standard benchmark datasets were about four-fifths lighter-skinned, and three commercial systems had error rates of up to 34.7% for darker-skinned women against 0.8% for lighter-skinned men. Facial analysis only; three products, published 2018: the figures describe those products then, not AI in general. Only the abstract was read.

items.title: A Framework for Understanding Sources of Harm throughout the Machine Learning Life Cycle
items.publisher: Harini Suresh and John V. Guttag (arXiv; ACM EAAMO 2021)
items.quote: seven distinct potential sources of downstream harm in machine learning, spanning data collection, development, and deployment
items.why: A widely cited framework naming seven sources of harm across data collection, development and deployment. Useful as a checklist for what a screening step should look for, and as a corrective: not all harm comes from the data. Authors' preprint of a conference paper; conceptual, not an empirical study. Only the abstract was read.

items.title: Datasheets for Datasets
items.publisher: Timnit Gebru and others (arXiv; published in Communications of the ACM, December 2021)
items.quote: every dataset be accompanied with a datasheet that documents its motivation, composition, collection process, recommended uses, and so on
items.why: The origin of the practice of documenting a dataset's provenance and composition, which is what a buyer is asking for when it asks a supplier how training data was checked. A proposal, not evidence that datasheets reduce bias. Authors' preprint; only the abstract was read.
